title: What is known about 1RB0LC_1LA0RD_0LD1LF_0RE0RA_1LB1RE_0LB---
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0LC_1LA0RD_0LD1LF_0RE0RA_1LB1RE_0LB---.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. Lean proves no halt in the first 10,000 steps by the kernel alone and in the first 107 with native_decide; the C simulator finds no halt in the first 109 steps.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 62,238 cells have been visited and 34,910 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: fixed/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.451). Right of the start it stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half).

claims.title: Macro structure (observed)
claims.text: A layered bouncer: (011) segments separated by markers (01)^3 10110; the head converts the first segment into (110)s three for one, then counts the next level down, so each layer is about three times the one before (13, 44, 51, ... 646, 1115).

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. The decider pipeline of bbchallenge left it open; no proof either way is recorded here yet.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. Started on a blank tape, this Turing machine has run for 10<sup>9</sup> steps without stopping. This page runs the real machine in your browser, shows the shape of its run, and lists what is known, each result marked by what it rests on.

facts.text: No halt in the C simulator; 62,238 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.
The growth shape of the two sides of the tape (see below).

sections.heading: Layers, each three times the last
html: The tape is a stack of segments (011)^k separated by a fixed marker. In one phase the head turns the first segment into (110) words, three for every (011) it removes. In the other phase segments count down and up by small steps. Each layer is about three times the size of the one before: a ternary hierarchy.

This is read off long runs, not yet proved: the next step is to state these patterns as rules, prove them with tools/py/bbtools/symtm.py, and see whether the counters can ever reach the configuration that halts.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.451). Right of the start it stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half).
After 109 steps the tape spans 62,238 cells (44,792 left of the start, 5,553 right), with a density of 1s of 0.561.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

summary: A layered bouncer: (011) segments separated by markers (01)^3 10110; the head converts the first segment into (110)s three for one, then counts the next level down, so each layer is about three times the one before (13, 44, 51, ... 646, 1115).
